subject: mathematics
question_text: If A, B, C are the angles of a triangle, prove that sin 2A + sin 2B − sin 2C = 4 cos A cos B sin C.

mark_split.label: Pair two terms with a sum-to-product formula
Apply the product formula and conclude

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.97, chapter 8 TRANSFORMATIONS, Long Answer question 1(ii). The book prints TRANSFORMATIONS as a separate un-numbered chapter-style banner immediately after chapter 8's VSAQ run and restarts its numbering at 1; we ship both under one unit, ordered by the syllabus, and never mirror the book's arrangement. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+3+2+1+1 split rewards the two substantial transformations — the sum-to-product pairing and the use of the angle condition — over the set-up and the finish, and it is the same split and the same step ids already carried by the sibling cards of this family (sin2a_sum, cos2a_sum, sin_half_squares, cos_half_squares), deliberately: they are ONE method over different identities, so a student who learns the arc once can attempt any of them. IDENTITY CHECKED NUMERICALLY before and after writing, and every intermediate line of the derivation with it: at A = 50°, B = 60°, C = 70° both sides equal 1.2080455471, and the identity holds again at (40°, 75°, 65°) and (110°, 25°, 45°). Paper position: Maths-1A Section C carries the long answers at 8 marks each under the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27), any 2 of 3; the Transformations slot is always a question of this kind. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this identity — say the four moves in order, and where the angle condition gets used.

steps.label: State the angle condition
steps.margin_note: First mark. The minus sign in front of sin 2C is the only thing separating this question from the all-plus version, and it changes the answer from three sines to two cosines and a sine. Write the condition before any transformation.
steps.memory_tip: A + B = 180° − C. The angle carrying the minus sign is the one kept separate — here it is C.

recall.must_convey: That the angle condition is written down first, in the form the proof will actually use.
accept: write the angle condition first in the form the proof needs
state the given condition and rearrange it as A plus B equals one eighty minus C
note the angle sum before starting the transformation
modata angle condition rasi, kavalsina form lo pettali
write down the condition on the angles

steps.why: Without the condition the statement is false, so this line is not preamble — it is the hypothesis the whole proof depends on, and it is used twice below.
common_mistakes: Starting the transformation before writing the condition.
Writing the condition but never rearranging it into a usable form.

steps.label: Pair two terms
steps.margin_note: Three of the eight marks. The two terms carrying a PLUS sign are the pair; the term carrying the minus is expanded by the double angle formula instead. Quote each formula in brackets — the formulas are what the examiner marks.
steps.memory_tip: Pair the two plus terms, sin 2A with sin 2B. Expand the minus term sin 2C as 2 sinC cosC.
lines: [∵ sin p + sin q = 2 sin((p+q)/2) cos((p−q)/2)]

recall.must_convey: That the two PLUS terms are paired with the sin C + sin D formula, and the minus term is expanded by sin 2θ = 2 sinθ cosθ.
accept: pair the two plus terms with the sin C plus sin D formula and expand sin two C as two sin C cos C
apply sum to product on sin two A plus sin two B and the double angle on the third
combine the two terms that have a plus sign and expand the other one
modati rendu plus terms ni sum to product cheyyali, minus term double angle
use sinC plus sinD on the first pair

steps.why: Three terms will not factorise as they stand. Pairing two of them makes a product, and the third term is expanded so that it can share a factor with that product.
common_mistakes: Losing the minus sign in front of sin 2C when the double angle formula is applied.
Using the sine sum formula on two terms that carry opposite signs.

steps.label: Use the condition
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. This is where the angle condition is used: it converts an expression in A and B into one in C, so that both terms carry the same factor 2 sin C.
steps.memory_tip: sin(180° − C) = +sin C. Sine keeps its sign across 180°; only the cosine changes sign.

recall.must_convey: That A + B is replaced by 180° − C, and sin(180° − C) simplifies to sin C — which is what makes the two terms share a factor.
accept: replace A plus B by one eighty minus C and sin of one eighty minus C is sin C
use the angle condition so both terms carry sin C
substitute the angle sum so sin A plus B becomes sin C
A plus B ni one eighty minus C ga marchi, sin C vasthundi
convert using the supplementary angle

steps.why: sin(180° − θ) = sin θ is what turns sin(A+B) into sin C. Without the angle condition the two terms would never share a factor.
common_mistakes: Writing sin(180° − C) = −sin C, which is the cosine rule not the sine one.
Forgetting to use the condition at all.

steps.label: Take the common factor out
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. The common factor 2 sin C comes out, and the condition is used a SECOND time inside the bracket so that the bracket becomes a SUM of two cosines rather than a difference.
steps.memory_tip: Take 2 sinC out. Then cos C = −cos(A+B) turns the minus inside the bracket into a plus.

recall.must_convey: That 2 sin C is taken out as a common factor, and cos C is rewritten as −cos(A+B) so the bracket becomes a sum of cosines.
accept: take two sin C common then rewrite cos C as minus cos A plus B so the bracket adds
factor out two sin C and convert the cosine using the angle sum again
the common factor comes out and the bracket becomes cos A minus B plus cos A plus B
two sin C common teesi, cos C ni minus cos A plus B ga marchali
use the condition a second time on the cosine

steps.why: The bracket has to become a SUM of cosines, because only a sum of cosines gives a product of cosines, and the right-hand side needs cos A cos B.
common_mistakes: Writing cos(180° − θ) = +cos θ, which leaves the bracket as a difference.
Taking out sin C instead of 2 sin C.

steps.label: Apply the product formula
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The SUM formula turns the bracket into a product of two cosines and the proof is finished. Write "= R.H.S" so the examiner can see the last line reaches the right-hand side.
steps.memory_tip: A SUM of two cosines gives a product of two cosines. A difference would have given sines.

recall.must_convey: That cos(A+B) + cos(A−B) = 2 cosA cosB is applied, giving 4 cosA cosB sinC.
accept: use cos A plus B plus cos A minus B equals two cos A cos B to get four cos A cos B sin C
the bracket becomes two cos A cos B so the answer is four cos A cos B sin C
apply the cosine sum formula to finish
cos sum formula tho two cos A cos B vasthundi, four cos A cos B sin C
the last formula gives four cos A cos B sin C
heard_as: four cos A cos B sin C

steps.why: cos(A+B) + cos(A−B) = 2 cos A cos B supplies the two cosine factors the right-hand side needs, and the sin C is the factor already taken out.
common_mistakes: Using the difference formula, which gives sines instead of cosines.
Stopping at the bracket without applying the formula.
